scope: 3.3.1–3.3.6 Year 1 organic compulsory curriculum, 19 numbered subsections; sampled atomic checks are not a guarantee that every AQA learning outcome or skill has been certified.

rows.requirement: Meanings of empirical, molecular, displayed and skeletal formulae

cards.front: What is an empirical formula?
cards.back: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element.

cards.front: What is a molecular formula?
cards.back: Actual number of atoms of each element per molecule.

cards.front: What does 'displayed formula' show?
cards.back: Every atom and every covalent bond.

cards.front: What is a skeletal formula?
cards.back: A line representation omitting C symbols and most attached H atoms.

rows.requirement: Characteristics of a homologous series and successive CH2 units

cards.front: What is a homologous series?
cards.back: Compounds with the same functional group and general formula.

cards.front: What changes by CH₂ from one member of a homologous series to the next?
cards.back: The carbon chain length.

rows.requirement: Interpret carbon positions and attached hydrogens in skeletal formulae

cards.front: In a skeletal formula, what does each unlabelled line end represent?
cards.back: One carbon atom.

cards.front: In a skeletal formula, how many bonds does neutral carbon normally make?
cards.back: Four covalent bonds, with omitted C–H bonds implied.

rows.requirement: Name straightforward organic chains with substituents

cards.front: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
cards.back: 2-methylbutane.

cards.front: Name CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
cards.back: Butan-2-ol.

rows.limitation: Examples are short, not the full six-carbon chains-and-rings range.

rows.requirement: Draw structural, displayed and skeletal structures from unfamiliar names up to six carbons and rings

cards.front: What is a skeletal formula?
cards.back: A line representation omitting C symbols and most attached H atoms.

cards.front: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
cards.back: 2-methylbutane.

questions.prompt: For CH₃CH=CHCH₂OH: give the correct IUPAC name, explain whether E/Z isomerism is possible, and state a reliable method for determining E or Z from a displayed drawing.
markPoints: Principal functional group is the alcohol: number chain from the –CH₂OH end.
Name is but-2-en-1-ol.
Each C=C carbon has two different substituents, so E/Z is possible.
Compare atomic numbers of directly attached atoms; move outward after ties.
Higher priorities same side gives Z; opposite sides gives E.

rows.limitation: The drawing question is one sample, not a systematic variety of named rings and functional groups.

rows.requirement: Distinguish a general formula from a specific structural formula

cards.front: What is the general formula for an acyclic alkane?
cards.back: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

cards.front: What does 'displayed formula' show?
cards.back: Every atom and every covalent bond.

rows.limitation: General formula is illustrated through alkanes but the contrast is not directly tested.

rows.requirement: Radical dots and distinction between homolytic and heterolytic fission

cards.front: What is homolytic fission?
cards.back: Each atom takes one electron from the covalent bond, forming radicals.

cards.front: What is heterolytic fission?
cards.back: Both bonding electrons go to one atom, forming ions.

cards.front: In a radical mechanism, what does a dot after a symbol mean?
cards.back: An unpaired electron, not an ionic charge.

rows.requirement: Show electron-pair movement using curly-arrow origins and direction

cards.front: Where should the tail of a curly arrow be placed?
cards.back: At an electron pair: a lone pair or covalent bond.

cards.front: When a C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, where does its curly arrow point?
cards.back: Towards Br, which takes the bonding electron pair.

cards.front: Choose the correct arrow source: A electrophile; B lone pair; C positive charge.
cards.back: B: the lone pair supplying the electrons.

rows.requirement: Write a complete balanced sequence of radical initiation, propagation and termination steps

cards.front: Radical initiation: fill the gap, Cl₂ → ___ (under UV).
cards.back: 2Cl•

cards.front: Radical propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + ___
cards.back: CH₃•

cards.front: Radical propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + ___
cards.back: Cl•

questions.prompt: On paper set out the initiation, two propagation and two different termination equations for free-radical chlorination of methane. Explain why it is a chain reaction and why a mixture can form.
markPoints: Initiation under UV: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.
Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•.
Propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
Valid termination: Cl• + CH₃• → CH₃Cl (or equivalent).
Different valid termination: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ (or Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂).
Radicals are regenerated in propagation, sustaining a chain.
Further substitution or alternative terminations give a product mixture.

rows.requirement: Draw ionic mechanisms showing intermediate charges and every relevant arrow

cards.front: When a C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, where does its curly arrow point?
cards.back: Towards Br, which takes the bonding electron pair.

questions.prompt: A student draws OH⁻ attacking the Br atom in CH₃CH₂Br. Explain why this is wrong and draw or describe the corrected two-curly-arrow substitution mechanism, including product ions.
markPoints: C–Br is polar; its carbon is δ⁺.
OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile, donating a lone pair from O.
Arrow from O lone pair to the carbon attached to Br (not to Br).
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, forming Br⁻.
Organic product is ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.

questions.prompt: A halogenoalkane RBr reacts with ammonia to give a primary amine. Draw or describe the two stages with all charges, the initially formed organic ion and the subsequent proton transfer.
markPoints: NH₃ is a neutral nucleophile with a nitrogen lone pair.
Arrow from the N lone pair to the δ⁺ carbon bonded to Br.
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, which leaves as Br⁻.
The first organic intermediate is positively charged RNH₃⁺.
A second ammonia molecule accepts a proton from RNH₃⁺.
The organic product is RNH₂, a primary amine; NH₄⁺ is also formed.

questions.prompt: 2-Bromobutane can undergo elimination. Draw the concerted elimination mechanism on paper (or explain all three curly arrows). Identify the organic product types and why more than one alkene is possible.
markPoints: OH⁻ acts as a base and accepts a hydrogen from a β carbon.
First arrow: O lone pair of OH⁻ to a β hydrogen.
Second arrow: β C–H bond pair to the C–C bond, forming C=C.
Third arrow: C–Br bond electron pair to Br, giving Br⁻.
Products include an alkene, water and Br⁻.
Removing H from either adjacent carbon allows but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene has E/Z forms.

rows.requirement: Define structural isomers, stereoisomers and their structural relationship

cards.front: What is a structural isomer?
cards.back: Same molecular formula, different structural formula.

cards.front: How is stereoisomerism different from structural isomerism?
cards.back: Same connectivity but a different arrangement in space.

rows.requirement: Distinguish chain, position and functional-group isomerism

cards.front: What is a position isomer?
cards.back: Same skeleton and group type, but in a different position.

cards.front: What is chain isomerism?
cards.back: Same molecular formula but a different carbon skeleton.

cards.front: What is a functional-group isomer?
cards.back: Same molecular formula but different functional groups.

rows.requirement: State E/Z conditions and interpret E and Z using priority groups

cards.front: What condition permits E/Z isomerism around a C=C bond?
cards.back: Each double-bond carbon has two different groups.

cards.front: What does E mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
cards.back: Higher-priority groups are on opposite sides.

cards.front: What does Z mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
cards.back: Higher-priority groups are on the same side.

rows.requirement: Apply CIP ranking including a tie at the first attached atom

cards.front: How are priorities assigned using CIP rules?
cards.back: Higher atomic number of the directly attached atom gets higher priority; move outward at the first difference.

cards.front: In CIP ranking, if attached atoms tie, what do you compare next?
cards.back: Their attached atoms, ordered by atomic number, until the first difference.

cards.front: CIP: which has higher priority, –CH₂OH or –CH₃?
cards.back: –CH₂OH: its next attached atoms include oxygen.

rows.requirement: Draw and classify unfamiliar E/Z pairs and other isomers

cards.front: How is stereoisomerism different from structural isomerism?
cards.back: Same connectivity but a different arrangement in space.

cards.front: In CIP ranking, if attached atoms tie, what do you compare next?
cards.back: Their attached atoms, ordered by atomic number, until the first difference.

questions.prompt: For CH₃CH=CHCH₂OH: give the correct IUPAC name, explain whether E/Z isomerism is possible, and state a reliable method for determining E or Z from a displayed drawing.
markPoints: Principal functional group is the alcohol: number chain from the –CH₂OH end.
Name is but-2-en-1-ol.
Each C=C carbon has two different substituents, so E/Z is possible.
Compare atomic numbers of directly attached atoms; move outward after ties.
Higher priorities same side gives Z; opposite sides gives E.

rows.requirement: Define an alkane as a saturated hydrocarbon

cards.front: Define an alkane.
cards.back: A saturated hydrocarbon containing only carbon–carbon single bonds.

rows.requirement: Explain fractionation using boiling ranges and the temperature gradient

cards.front: What is a crude-oil fraction?
cards.back: A mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.

cards.front: Fill the gap: a fractionating column is cooler near the ___.
cards.back: top

cards.front: Where do higher-boiling crude-oil fractions condense?
cards.back: Lower down the hotter fractionating column.

cards.front: Is fractional distillation a chemical change or physical separation?
cards.back: Physical separation; no hydrocarbon molecules are changed.

rows.requirement: Relate alkane boiling-point trend to London forces

cards.front: Why do larger alkane molecules generally have higher boiling points?
cards.back: More electrons produce stronger London dispersion forces.

rows.requirement: Define cracking and distinguish thermal from catalytic cracking

cards.front: What is cracking?
cards.back: Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.

cards.front: What distinguishes thermal from catalytic cracking in product emphasis?
cards.back: Thermal cracking favours alkenes; catalytic cracking favours fuels and aromatics.

cards.front: Which cracking method uses high temperature and high pressure?
cards.back: Thermal cracking.

cards.front: Fill the gap: catalytic cracking uses a ___ catalyst.
cards.back: zeolite

rows.requirement: Recall zeolite and catalytic cracking product emphasis

cards.front: What catalyst is associated with catalytic cracking and what products are valuable?
cards.back: A zeolite catalyst; valuable products include motor fuels and aromatic hydrocarbons.

rows.requirement: Explain industrial economic reason for cracking heavier fractions

cards.front: What is the economic reason for cracking long-chain alkane fractions?
cards.back: To convert less-demanded heavy fractions into more useful, higher-demand fuels and chemical feedstocks.

rows.requirement: Apply atom-balance ideas to unfamiliar cracking product equations

cards.front: What is cracking?
cards.back: Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.

rows.limitation: Existing prompts recall cracking rather than checking unfamiliar balanced product equations.

rows.requirement: Distinguish complete and incomplete hydrocarbon combustion products

cards.front: What is complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
cards.back: Reaction with sufficient oxygen producing CO₂ and H₂O.

cards.front: What carbon-containing products can form in incomplete hydrocarbon combustion?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide (CO) and solid carbon (soot); some CO₂ may also form.

rows.requirement: Explain why nitrogen oxides form in vehicle engines

cards.front: Why can nitrogen oxides form inside combustion engines?
cards.back: High temperatures allow nitrogen and oxygen from air to react.

rows.requirement: Identify roles of oxidation and reduction in catalytic converters

cards.front: In a catalytic converter, CO is oxidised to which gas?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide, CO₂.

cards.front: In a catalytic converter, nitrogen oxides are reduced to what?
cards.back: Nitrogen, N₂.

rows.requirement: Explain removing sulfur dioxide using oxide and carbonate chemistry

cards.front: Complete the flue-gas equation: CaO + SO₂ → ___
cards.back: CaSO₃.

cards.front: Complete the flue-gas equation: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + ___
cards.back: CO₂.

rows.requirement: Evaluate multiple pollutants and relevant environmental consequences from a case study

cards.front: What carbon-containing products can form in incomplete hydrocarbon combustion?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide (CO) and solid carbon (soot); some CO₂ may also form.

cards.front: Why can nitrogen oxides form inside combustion engines?
cards.back: High temperatures allow nitrogen and oxygen from air to react.

rows.limitation: Individual emissions appear as recall, but a combined case-study justification is not evidenced here.

rows.requirement: Complete the stages of methane chlorination as a radical chain

cards.front: Radical initiation: fill the gap, Cl₂ → ___ (under UV).
cards.back: 2Cl•

cards.front: Radical propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + ___
cards.back: CH₃•

cards.front: Termination: complete CH₃• + CH₃• → ___
cards.back: C₂H₆.

questions.prompt: On paper set out the initiation, two propagation and two different termination equations for free-radical chlorination of methane. Explain why it is a chain reaction and why a mixture can form.
markPoints: Initiation under UV: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.
Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•.
Propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
Valid termination: Cl• + CH₃• → CH₃Cl (or equivalent).
Different valid termination: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ (or Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂).
Radicals are regenerated in propagation, sustaining a chain.
Further substitution or alternative terminations give a product mixture.

rows.requirement: Explain multiple substitution and mixture of products

cards.front: Why can methane chlorination give several chlorinated products?
cards.back: The products can undergo further radical substitution.

rows.requirement: Explain polar C–halogen bond and electrophilic carbon

cards.front: What bond property makes halogenoalkanes reactive?
cards.back: The C–halogen bond is polar.

cards.front: Why is the C atom bonded to a halogen electrophilic?
cards.back: Bond polarisation gives that carbon a partial positive charge.

rows.requirement: Identify product classes for OH– and CN– substitution

cards.front: What is the main type of product from nucleophilic substitution by OH⁻?
cards.back: An alcohol.

cards.front: What is the organic product type from substitution by CN⁻?
cards.back: A nitrile.

cards.front: When CN⁻ replaces a halogen in R–X, how does the carbon count change?
cards.back: It increases by one carbon atom.

rows.requirement: Draw nucleophilic substitution including bond-breaking arrow

cards.front: Substitution arrow 1: OH⁻ attacks which atom of a halogenoalkane?
cards.back: The δ⁺ carbon bonded to the halogen.

cards.front: Substitution arrow 2: where does the C–Br bond's electron pair move?
cards.back: To bromine, which leaves as Br⁻.

questions.prompt: A student draws OH⁻ attacking the Br atom in CH₃CH₂Br. Explain why this is wrong and draw or describe the corrected two-curly-arrow substitution mechanism, including product ions.
markPoints: C–Br is polar; its carbon is δ⁺.
OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile, donating a lone pair from O.
Arrow from O lone pair to the carbon attached to Br (not to Br).
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, forming Br⁻.
Organic product is ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.

rows.requirement: Track NH3 intermediate charges and proton transfer on a structure

cards.front: Fill the gap: substitution of R–Br with NH₃ first gives R–NH₃___.
What happens after the positively charged RNH₃⁺ intermediate forms?
cards.back: A base removes H⁺, giving a neutral primary amine.

questions.prompt: A halogenoalkane RBr reacts with ammonia to give a primary amine. Draw or describe the two stages with all charges, the initially formed organic ion and the subsequent proton transfer.
markPoints: NH₃ is a neutral nucleophile with a nitrogen lone pair.
Arrow from the N lone pair to the δ⁺ carbon bonded to Br.
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, which leaves as Br⁻.
The first organic intermediate is positively charged RNH₃⁺.
A second ammonia molecule accepts a proton from RNH₃⁺.
The organic product is RNH₂, a primary amine; NH₄⁺ is also formed.

rows.requirement: Relate hydrolysis rates to C–halogen bond enthalpy and comparative data

cards.front: Why do iodoalkanes generally hydrolyse faster than chloroalkanes?
cards.back: The C–I bond has lower bond enthalpy.

questions.prompt: Three otherwise comparable halogenoalkanes show an observable silver-halide precipitate after 45 s (iodo), 90 s (bromo), and 180 s (chloro). Rank their apparent rates, calculate the ratio of the fastest and slowest times, and explain the trend and a limitation of timing precipitate appearance.
markPoints: Order of apparent hydrolysis speed is iodo > bromo > chloro.
Time ratio slowest/fastest = 180/45 = 4.
C–I has a lower bond enthalpy than C–Br or C–Cl.
Weaker C–X bond makes hydrolysis more rapid for otherwise comparable structures.
First visible precipitate time gives an approximate comparison, not an exact initial rate.

rows.requirement: Explain how hydroxide can act as nucleophile or base

cards.front: Why may the same species be a base in one reaction and nucleophile in another?
cards.back: It may accept H+ or donate an electron pair to carbon, respectively.

cards.front: In elimination by OH⁻, does OH⁻ attack carbon or an adjacent hydrogen?
cards.back: An adjacent (β) hydrogen; OH⁻ acts as a base.

rows.requirement: Draw all electron movements in halogenoalkane elimination

cards.front: Elimination arrow 1: where does the oxygen lone pair of OH⁻ point?
cards.back: To a hydrogen on the carbon next to the C–Br carbon.

cards.front: Elimination arrow 2: where do the β C–H bonding electrons move?
cards.back: Into the bond between the two carbons, forming C=C.

cards.front: Elimination arrow 3: where do the C–Br bonding electrons move?
cards.back: To Br, forming Br⁻.

questions.prompt: 2-Bromobutane can undergo elimination. Draw the concerted elimination mechanism on paper (or explain all three curly arrows). Identify the organic product types and why more than one alkene is possible.
markPoints: OH⁻ acts as a base and accepts a hydrogen from a β carbon.
First arrow: O lone pair of OH⁻ to a β hydrogen.
Second arrow: β C–H bond pair to the C–C bond, forming C=C.
Third arrow: C–Br bond electron pair to Br, giving Br⁻.
Products include an alkene, water and Br⁻.
Removing H from either adjacent carbon allows but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene has E/Z forms.

rows.requirement: Identify possible positional isomers from elimination

cards.front: Elimination of 2-bromobutane: name two possible alkene position isomers.
cards.back: But-1-ene and but-2-ene.

rows.requirement: Explain how CFC-derived chlorine radicals are generated by UV

cards.front: Why are CFCs damaging in the stratosphere?
cards.back: UV releases chlorine radicals that destroy ozone.

rows.requirement: Explain chlorine-radical catalysis and write linked ozone equations

cards.front: Ozone cycle step 1: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + ___
cards.back: O₂.

cards.front: Ozone cycle step 2: ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + ___
cards.back: 2O₂.

cards.front: Complete the net ozone-decomposition equation: 2O₃ → ___
cards.back: 3O₂.

questions.prompt: An exam question gives Cl• reacting with stratospheric ozone. Write the two radical steps and deduce the net equation. Explain why chlorine atoms are catalysts rather than reactants overall.
markPoints: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂.
ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂.
Cl• is consumed in one step but regenerated in the next.
ClO• is an intermediate and cancels when equations are summed.
Overall 2O₃ → 3O₂, with net ozone depletion.

rows.requirement: Explain upper-atmosphere ozone absorbing UV radiation
rows.limitation: A short direct definition and purpose question was not located in the audited topic-specific cards.

rows.requirement: Interpret research evidence and regulation of ozone-depleting CFCs

cards.front: Why are CFCs damaging in the stratosphere?
cards.back: UV releases chlorine radicals that destroy ozone.

rows.limitation: A causal flashcard is present, but not an evidence/legislation interpretation question.

rows.requirement: Explain high electron density in the carbon–carbon double bond

cards.front: Why is the alkene double bond attacked by electrophiles?
cards.back: The π bond has high electron density.

cards.front: An alkene C=C consists of which two bond types?
cards.back: One σ bond and one π bond.

rows.requirement: Recognise an alkene as unsaturated and explain restricted double-bond rotation

cards.front: What is the general formula for an acyclic monoalkene?
cards.back: CₙH₂ₙ.

cards.front: Why does a C=C bond restrict rotation?
cards.back: Rotation would disrupt sideways overlap forming the π bond.

rows.requirement: Draw electrophilic addition to ethene with HBr

cards.front: HBr addition arrow 2: where does the H–Br bond's electron pair go?
cards.back: To bromine, forming Br⁻.

cards.front: After HBr protonates ethene, which charged intermediate forms?
cards.back: The ethyl carbocation, CH₃CH₂⁺.

cards.front: HBr addition final arrow: where does the Br⁻ lone pair point?
cards.back: Towards the positively charged carbon of the carbocation.

questions.prompt: Ethene reacts with HBr. On paper draw the full electrophilic addition mechanism with charges and every curly arrow. Alternatively describe where each arrow starts and ends. Identify the organic product.
markPoints: Show Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻ (or otherwise identify the polar H–Br bond).
First curly arrow goes from C=C π bond towards the H atom.
Second curly arrow goes from the H–Br bond to Br, giving Br⁻.
Show the CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation intermediate with charge on carbon.
Arrow goes from a Br⁻ lone pair towards the carbocation carbon.
Final organic product is CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.

rows.requirement: Show the induced dipole and electron movements in Br2 addition

cards.front: Why does Br₂ become polarised as it approaches an alkene?
cards.back: The alkene π electrons repel Br₂ electrons, inducing a dipole.

cards.front: Br₂ addition arrow 1: where do the alkene π electrons move?
cards.back: Towards the induced δ⁺ bromine atom.

cards.front: Br₂ addition arrow 2: where do the Br–Br bonding electrons go?
cards.back: Towards the other Br, forming Br⁻.

questions.prompt: Bromine molecules are non-polar before they approach ethene. Explain their reaction and, on paper, draw a mechanism showing a polarised Br₂, the electron-pair movements and the product.
markPoints: C=C is an electron-rich π bond.
The π electrons induce a dipole in approaching Br₂; nearest Br becomes δ⁺.
Arrow from the C=C electron pair to the δ⁺ bromine atom.
Arrow from Br–Br bonding pair to the other bromine; Br⁻ forms.
A positively charged bromine-containing intermediate is attacked by Br⁻.
Product is CH₂BrCH₂Br, 1,2-dibromoethane.

rows.requirement: Account for addition of H2SO4 to an alkene

cards.front: What is the immediate product of ethene + H₂SO₄?
cards.back: Ethyl hydrogensulfate, CH₃CH₂OSO₃H.

cards.front: After H₂SO₄ protonates ethene, which ion attacks the carbocation?
cards.back: Hydrogensulfate, HSO₄⁻, through oxygen.

questions.prompt: Ethene undergoes electrophilic addition with H₂SO₄. Draw or describe the arrow movements, intermediates and immediate organic product; then state how that product relates to ethanol.
markPoints: Ethene's C=C π electrons attack an H of H₂SO₄.
The O–H bonding pair goes to oxygen, giving HSO₄⁻.
A CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation forms.
The HSO₄⁻ oxygen donates a lone pair to the carbocation carbon.
The immediate product is CH₃CH₂OSO₃H (ethyl hydrogensulfate).
Hydrolysis of the alkyl hydrogensulfate yields ethanol.

rows.requirement: Relate major/minor products to carbocation stability

cards.front: Order typical carbocations by stability.
cards.back: Tertiary is more stable than secondary, which is more stable than primary.

cards.front: In the major product from propene + HBr, which carbon bears bromine?
cards.back: Carbon 2 (forming 2-bromopropane).

questions.prompt: Propene reacts with HBr and produces two bromoalkane isomers. Draw or describe the two possible carbocations, give their classes and explain the major product using intermediate stability.
markPoints: One pathway forms a secondary carbocation: CH₃CH⁺CH₃.
The alternative pathway forms a primary carbocation: CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺.
The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary one.
Attack by Br⁻ on the secondary carbocation gives 2-bromopropane.
Identify 2-bromopropane as major and 1-bromopropane as minor.

rows.requirement: Interpret bromine-water decolourisation as evidence for unsaturation

cards.front: What colour change indicates an alkene with bromine water?
cards.back: Orange to colourless.

rows.requirement: Convert between substituted monomers and polymer repeat units

cards.back: Outside the square brackets.

Cl remains a side group, not in the backbone.
Continuation bonds pass through each side of the brackets.
Monomer is reconstructed as CH₂=CHCl by restoring the C=C.

cards.front: Why are addition polymers often chemically unreactive?

rows.requirement: Define biofuel and explain why production is not automatically carbon neutral

cards.front: What is a biofuel?

rows.requirement: Recognise primary, secondary and tertiary alcohol structures

cards.front: How do you identify a primary alcohol?
cards.back: Its C–OH carbon bonds to one or no other carbon atoms.

cards.front: How do you identify a secondary alcohol?
cards.back: Its C–OH carbon bonds to two other carbon atoms.

cards.front: How do you identify a tertiary alcohol?
cards.back: Its C–OH carbon bonds to three other carbon atoms.

rows.requirement: State oxidation products of primary and secondary alcohols

cards.front: What forms when a primary alcohol is oxidised gently and distilled?
cards.back: An aldehyde.

cards.front: What forms when a primary alcohol is oxidised under reflux with excess oxidant?
cards.back: A carboxylic acid.

cards.front: What forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidised?
cards.back: A ketone.

rows.requirement: Explain why tertiary alcohols resist common oxidation conditions

cards.front: Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to normal oxidation?
cards.back: No hydrogen on the carbon attached to –OH.

rows.requirement: Use orange-to-green oxidation observation and distinguish oxidation states

cards.front: Which colour change shows Cr₂O₇²⁻ reducing to Cr³⁺ in alcohol oxidation?
cards.back: Orange to green.

cards.front: Which oxidation state does chromium change from/to in dichromate oxidation?

rows.requirement: Explain reflux versus distillation for aldehyde isolation

cards.front: Why use distillation rather than reflux to isolate an aldehyde?
cards.back: Distillation removes the aldehyde before it can oxidise further.

cards.front: Why does reflux prevent loss of volatile reactants?
cards.back: Vapour condenses and returns to the reaction vessel.

questions.prompt: A student suggests reflux rather than distillation to isolate a volatile oxidation product, even though the product can oxidise further. Explain why this change is unsuitable and what general apparatus principles are important in interpreting distillation data.
markPoints: Reflux condenses vapour and returns it to the reaction mixture.
Returning product allows further oxidation instead of isolating it.
Distillation removes the more volatile product as it forms.
The thermometer should represent vapour entering the condenser, not liquid temperature.
The collected boiling range is evidence for identity/purity only with comparison data.

rows.requirement: Distinguish aldehydes and ketones using characteristic test observations

cards.front: Which test would show an aldehyde but not a typical simple ketone?
cards.back: Tollens' or Fehling's reagent gives a positive result.

questions.prompt: Two unknown substances X and Y each give a positive 2,4-DNPH test. X also gives a Tollens' silver deposit; Y does not. Explain the conclusions, including what 2,4-DNPH alone cannot establish.
markPoints: Positive 2,4-DNPH indicates a carbonyl of an aldehyde or ketone.
2,4-DNPH alone cannot distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone.
X is an aldehyde under these conditions because Tollens' is positive.
Y is consistent with a ketone because Tollens' is negative.
An independent test or spectrum can confirm identification.

rows.requirement: Explain acid-catalysed dehydration to an alkene with key electron movements

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration mechanism step 1: what happens to the –OH group?
cards.back: It is protonated to –OH₂⁺, making water a better leaving group.

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration: which proton is removed to form the C=C bond?
cards.back: A β-hydrogen on a carbon next to the former –OH carbon.

cards.front: During alcohol dehydration, which electrons form the alkene's π bond?
cards.back: A pair from a C–H bond next to the carbon losing water.

questions.prompt: A generic alcohol undergoes acid-catalysed dehydration to give an alkene. Describe the electron and proton changes or draw a schematic curly-arrow mechanism; explain why the acid is a catalyst.
markPoints: Alcohol oxygen is protonated so –OH becomes –OH₂⁺.
This makes neutral water a possible leaving group.
The molecule loses water and a β hydrogen, creating C=C.
Deprotonation restores a neutral organic product.
The H⁺ catalyst is regenerated overall.

rows.requirement: Recall regeneration of acid catalyst in dehydration

cards.front: Alcohol dehydration: what happens to the acid catalyst overall?
cards.back: It is regenerated.

rows.requirement: Connect alcohol-derived alkene polymers with reduced crude-oil dependence

cards.front: What forms when an alcohol undergoes dehydration?
cards.back: An alkene and water.

rows.limitation: Reaction facts exist, but the sustainability explanation needs applied evaluation.

rows.requirement: Identify unsaturation from bromine-water observations

cards.front: What is the test for an alkene?
cards.back: Bromine water is decolourised from orange/brown.

cards.front: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless in a functional-group test. What bond is suggested?
cards.back: A carbon–carbon double bond, C=C.

rows.requirement: Distinguish carboxylic acid via carbonate observations

cards.front: A positive carbonate–acid identification gives which observable sign?
cards.back: Bubbles of carbon dioxide.

cards.front: What class of organic compounds commonly gives CO₂ in a carbonate test?
cards.back: Carboxylic acids.

questions.prompt: Four unknown organic liquids show these results: A decolourises bromine water; B effervesces with carbonate; C oxidises acidified dichromate(VI) from orange to green but has no carbonyl test; D forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and gives a silver mirror. Identify the most likely functional group in each and one limitation of the evidence.
markPoints: A is consistent with an alkene (C=C) under the stated conditions.
B is consistent with a carboxylic acid, producing CO₂.
C is consistent with an oxidisable alcohol (primary or secondary).
D contains an aldehyde group (carbonyl plus positive Tollens').
Some tests are not exclusive, so confirmation with complementary evidence is needed.

rows.requirement: Distinguish aldehyde from ketone with paired positive and negative tests

cards.front: What extra evidence can distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.back: A positive Tollens’ or Fehling’s result indicates an aldehyde.

questions.prompt: Two unknown substances X and Y each give a positive 2,4-DNPH test. X also gives a Tollens' silver deposit; Y does not. Explain the conclusions, including what 2,4-DNPH alone cannot establish.
markPoints: Positive 2,4-DNPH indicates a carbonyl of an aldehyde or ketone.
2,4-DNPH alone cannot distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone.
X is an aldehyde under these conditions because Tollens' is positive.
Y is consistent with a ketone because Tollens' is negative.
An independent test or spectrum can confirm identification.

rows.requirement: Interpret alcohol oxidation observations without overclaiming the alcohol class

cards.front: Can the orange-to-green oxidation observation alone distinguish primary from secondary alcohols?
cards.back: No; both types can be oxidised.

cards.front: Why is no orange-to-green change consistent with a tertiary alcohol?
cards.back: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under standard test conditions.

cards.front: How can a high-resolution mass spectrum help find a molecular formula?
cards.back: Its precise molecular mass can distinguish elemental compositions.

rows.requirement: Use precise atomic masses to decide molecular formula between candidates

cards.front: How can a high-resolution mass spectrum help find a molecular formula?
cards.back: Its precise molecular mass can distinguish elemental compositions.

rows.requirement: Identify major functional-group absorptions from IR data

cards.front: What does a broad O–H infrared absorption suggest?
cards.back: An alcohol or carboxylic acid.

cards.front: What does a strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ suggest?
cards.back: A carbonyl C=O group.

rows.requirement: Explain fingerprint comparison and recognizing impurity peaks

cards.front: What does a fingerprint region help identify?
cards.back: A specific compound by comparing its IR spectrum.

cards.front: How can an IR spectrum help reveal an impurity?
cards.back: It may show additional absorption peaks absent from the pure compound.

rows.requirement: Combine IR and organic observations without asserting unique identification

cards.front: Why is one positive functional-group test insufficient for an exact identity?
cards.back: Many molecules share that functional group.

questions.prompt: A molecular sample has a strong IR absorption around 1700 cm⁻¹, no very broad O–H absorption from 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, and gives no Tollens' silver deposit. Explain the most likely carbonyl class and the limitations of each clue.
markPoints: Absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O bond.
No broad acid O–H feature makes a carboxylic acid less likely.
Negative Tollens' result makes an ordinary aldehyde less likely.
A ketone is the most likely class under these conditions.
IR and chemical tests should be interpreted together; neither alone proves a unique structure.

rows.requirement: Explain greenhouse IR absorption by carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour

cards.front: Why can CO₂ and methane contribute to global warming?
cards.back: They absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from Earth.

cards.front: How does an IR spectrum help identify a functional group?
cards.back: Characteristic bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers.
